items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Juice was playing clarinet also and I used to sit in for a couple of numbers with his group.

ctx.x: I learned quite a lot from those contests because sometimes there were 3 or 4 trumpet players in the room and no-one played the piano. So we would see who knew how to do some difficult exercises that the others could not do. I learned how to jump from 'C' below the staff to the one above in the back room of the saloon, from a young trumpetplayer who had a style like Joe Smith. They used to have sessions of the [at] Rhythm Club in New York. One week, it would be for trumpet players, and different trumpet players…

It was also in Buffalo that I heard the greatest jazz violinist that ever lived. His name was Robert "Juice" Wilson. Juice played in a ballroom not far from the saloon where the musicians congregated and I went to listen to him almost every night before going to the saloon after I had finished work at the Arcadia. Juice worked until about 4 a.m, and we finished at 2 a.m.

I had not heard many jazz violinists because voilins were not played as a jazz instrument, although there were some orchestras that used violins in a very commercial way in some arrangements. I've heard the best jazz violinist since the first time I've heard Juice and to my estimation, there never was one greater than Robert "Juice" Wilson
